summary:
Daegu's visitor-relevant signal is concentrated in the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, held every June since 2009 without interruption and described as the country's second-largest LGBT event: a pride parade and film festival running a week or two, usually in late June. The city stands under the national framework of South Korea for criminal law, legal gender recognition, documents and healthcare; the findings below are those specific to Daegu.

Opposition is organised, annual and large. A Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual "National Assembly Against Queer" in response to the festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups have formed a "gay issue countermeasure committee" in Daegu to block LGBT events, and that opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street.

Court bids to stop the festival have failed each year. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee sought an injunction against the 2025 edition; the court dismissed it, as it had dismissed the bids for 2022, 2023 and 2024. In 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. Police again restricted the 2025 march to a single bus-only lane. Organisers framed the event as resistance to "hate and discriminatory politics".

The dispute continued into the 2026 edition. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, made up of the Daegu-Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of venue, arguing the event is likely to infringe public welfare. The group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single commission petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It responds to the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act.
tangentialFactors:
The counter-mobilisation is organised at Daegu-Gyeongbuk scale rather than city scale: the umbrella body draws churches from the surrounding province as well as the city, and the 2025 assembly was billed as a national gathering. The venue dispute has been routed through national institutions, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea, the National Police Agency and the National Assembly, rather than settled by the city.

Daegu's festival is the second-largest LGBT event in South Korea, so the annual pattern of injunction bids and police route limits is a comparator for visitors planning around other Korean pride events, though the specific restrictions described here are Daegu's own.
localsOnly:
For residents, the festival and its counter-assembly recur on a predictable June calendar in the city centre, around Jungang-ro and Banwoldang, with police route restrictions on the march and a single bus-only lane allocated to it. The Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, representing businesses in a central commercial district, is a named party to the opposition petition.

Injunction bids against the festival have been filed and dismissed each year since at least 2022, so the legal challenge is a recurring annual event rather than a one-off.
outOfScopeNotes:
The size of the counter-mobilisation and of the petition rests on the organisers' own figures: the 3,500 participants, 1,600 churches and 34,000 signatures are not independently verified in the sources. The outcome of the 2026 petition before the National Human Rights Commission of Korea is not sourced, and the sources do not detail whether police route restrictions differed in years other than 2025.

No Daegu-specific data was identified on violence against transgender people, healthcare access, document or marker practice, or facilities such as restrooms; those matters are carried by the national record for South Korea. National attitude survey figures cited alongside coverage of the festival are country-level and belong to the national record.
